pk/math.text: Counts forward to 20 by memory
Counts backwards from 5
Shows accuracy in demonstrating oneto-one correspondence for up to 10 objects
Counts up to 10 objects in a line
Answers the question “How many?” for up to 10 objects
Counts out 10-20 objects in a line from a larger group
Instantly recognizes a collection of up to 10 objects (i.e. subitizes)
Uses words that mean zero such as “nothing” or “none”
Shows a quantity to match a numeral by making marks, drawing items, or placing actual objects
Compares sets of objects that range in size from 1-10, as having “more”, “fewer” or “same”
Arranges images with 3 or more different quantities of objects in correct order
Solves addition (joining) problems using manipulatives (e.g., fingers, objects, tally marks)
Solves subtraction (separating) problems using manipulatives (e.g., fingers, objects, tally marks)
With adult help, uses “counting on” as a strategy to solve addition (joining) problems (e.g., “I have 3 and 2 more gives me 4, 5”)
With adult help, uses “counting back from” as a strategy to solve subtraction (separating) problems (e.g., To take away 3 from 5, “5,4,3...leaves 2”)
Uses smaller shapes to compose larger and different shapes (e.g., two triangles make one square)
Correctly names squares, rectangles and triangles regardless of size or orientation
Describes attributes of two and three dimensional shapes (e.g., “A square has four corners/angles”, “a triangle has three straight sides”)
Draws and describes pictures that show relative locations and uses terms like “near to” or “closer to”
Identifies, duplicates, extends, and creates simple repeating patterns
Fills in missing elements of simple, repeating patterns
Recognizes, names, and extends simple repeating patterns
Describes quantitative changes (e.g., “I am two years older than when I started school.”)
Directly compares the length or volume of two objects
Uses comparative language to describe and compare objects using attributes (e.g., longer, shorter, lighter, heavier, etc.)
With adult support, measures using the same non-standard unit, such as putting together snap cubes to see how tall a book is
With adult support, compares or orders up to 5 objects based on their measurable attributes, such as height or weight
With adult support, recognizes that different attributes such as weight, height, and volume require different tools to measure
With adult support, demonstrates “size seriation” by comparing and ordering objects according to measured attribute/ characteristic (e.g., places books on shelf according to measured size)
With adult support, explores tools of measurement such as rulers, scales, and measuring cup, using the appropriate tool for the attribute/characteristic being measured
With instruction, shows an awareness of time by talking about events with words such as before, after, and later

pk/language.text: Answers questions and adds comments relevant to the topic
Begins to demonstrate understanding of implied messages based on speaker’s tone and/ or gestures (e.g., finger on lip and saying “shhhh” means be quiet)
Understands and responds to words for descriptive concepts (e.g., hard, square)
Follows 2-3 step related directions and some new directions related to familiar and daily routines

Demonstrates understanding of communication that includes a variety of complex sentences related to familiar stories, learning activities, and events (e.g., After Clifford the dog came home, he played with Emily Elizabeth.)
Uses age-appropriate grammar in conversations and increasingly complex phrases and sentences (e.g., uses irregular past tense verbs such as came, ran, fell, broke, went, told, did)
Answers open-ended questions comfortably
Retells stories and events in sequence with multiple details (e.g., retells The Three Bears noting three chairs, three beds, etc.)
Begins to match language to contexts (e.g., voice volume, inflection/rise and fall of voice in speaking, and parting/greeting rituals)
Engages in multiple back-and-forth conversations with adults in ways that can be goal directed (such as solving problems)
Asks and responds to questions with accurate information
Distinguishes among a variety of texts and their purposes (e.g., books, shopping lists, etc.)
Begins to track individual words in text or braille by pointing or touching
Listens and responds to a variety of texts and media (e.g., audio book, music and movement)
Tells fictional or personal stories sequentially and with 3 or more details
Begins to understand cause and effect relationships in fiction and nonfiction texts
Predicts what will happen next in an unfamiliar story
Uses new words learned through listening to stories
Begins to rhyme and produce rhymes of simple words
Begins to orally segment and combine compound words (e.g., lunchbox segmented is lunch-box; when combined it is lunchbox)
Begins to segment and combine syllables (e.g., purple segmented is purple; when combined it is purple)
Begins to identify the initial and final sound in words (e.g., /b/ in bat)
For many, with instructional support, matches the sound with the corresponding letter
For many, with instructional support, matches the letter with the corresponding sound
Recognizes many upper and lower case letters
Will use a combination of letters and symbols to represent words

pk/science.text: Compares and categorizes observable phenomena (e.g., by collecting, organizing, and describing materials according to their physical characteristics)
Imitates and uses adults’ words and ideas when talking about the physical and natural worlds
Shows detail in drawings, constructions, demonstrations to show thinking
Uses many sources (e.g., pictures, books) to gather information
With adult guidance, plans and conducts investigations
Analyzes results, draws conclusions, and communicates results
Collaborates with others to conduct investigations

Collaborates with others to conduct investigations

Communicates about the roles of people in the community encountered directly (caregiver or educator) and roles introduced through pictures, books and other media (artists, cooks, cashiers, construction workers)
Uses props and dramatic play to show growing awareness of things and events in the larger world (using a computer, driving a bus)
Shows more detail in drawings, buildings, models, and performances, reflecting their thinking and understanding about social connections
Communicates about self as member of many different groups, such as within a family, classroom, faith community, or sport team
Uses positive social behaviors (taking turns, sharing, helping with jobs) to help meet needs of the group
With adult help, participates with peers in solving problems, settling conflicts, and negotiating plans and decisions
Learns simple vocabulary of other languages spoken in home, classroom, or school community
Represents self and others in drawing with increasing detail and accuracy, including distinguishing features related to physical, racial, and cultural differences
With adult help, notices and communicates about different family structures represented in the group
Communicates about own family’s culture and traditions and accepts that children and families are different

Shares other identifying information (e.g., parent’s name)
Describes a larger range of individual characteristics and interests and communicates how these are similar or different from those of other people
Displays pride in their accomplishments
Acts independently in unfamiliar settings with unfamiliar adults
Attempts to complete tasks independently
Asks for support from adults only when needed
Begins to recognize their own emotions before reacting (e.g., pauses and takes deep breath when mad)
Communicates how other children or adults may be feeling and why (e.g., states that a peer is sad because their toy was taken away)
Recognizes appropriate reaction to situations
Uses words and respectful language to express thoughts and emotions (e.g., “I’m frustrated because Jay won’t let me play” or “I’m excited to play with my cousin Santiago tomorrow.”)
Demonstrates confidence in meeting own needs
Seeks and accepts help when needed
Increasingly uses a variety of strategies to self-soothe or solve problems (e.g., goes to a quiet area or uses a fidget toy when upset)
Exhibits emotional control with or without adult support (e.g., follows group activities although upset)
Shows care and concern for others, including comforting others in distress
Begins to recognize the emotions of peers and responds with empathy and compassion
Begins to understand the reasons for others’ emotions and responds appropriately (e.g., a child comforts a peer who is upset that they have to clean up their toys)
Shows enjoyment in interactions with trusted adults while also demonstrating skills in separating from these adults
Comfortable with being with less familiar adults in a safe setting (e.g., engages with visitor to home or classroom)
Demonstrates strategies for participating in social play with peers (e.g., asks to join in game or brings new item to add to existing play)
Plays with peers in a coordinated manner including assigning roles, materials, and actions (e.g., sets up and assigns roles in restaurant in dramatic play area)
Maintains friendships over time
Responds to the needs of others and tries to help others with simple tasks
Builds on cooperative play, communication, and working memory skills by engaging in dramatic play with several other children, each taking on a particular role in a shared theme
Engages in prosocial behavior such as cooperating, compromising, turntaking, and resolving social conflict
Expresses feelings and needs in conflict situations (e.g., “I’m feeling upset because you have the truck I need for my racetrack.”)
Uses problem-solving strategies independently or with adult prompting when feeling angry or frustrated (e.g., asks peer to trade toys because they want the one-of-a-kind toy)
